newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook - Surplus supplies bear down.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook - Surplus supplies bear down.

text.p: Singapore refiners might be forced to cut production sooner rather than later after Singapore gas oil broke down through support, traders said on Monday.
But production cuts might only boost sentiment temporarily, rather than tightening the Asian products market, suffering from high stocks and weak demand, they said.
Singapore oil refiners said last week they were facing operating losses for the first time in four months because of squeezed margins.
But on Friday gas oil, the bear of the barrel, pierced $25.00 per barrel support for the first time since August. It traded three times at $24.90.
Traders said $24.50 was next support, indicating refinery margins were tightening another critical notch amid generally steady crude prices.
Refinery profit margins turned positive within one month in January when refiners cut production between five and 20 percent in the face of negative margins.
But this time, some traders said they were skeptical whether cuts would be able to offset brimming stocks around the region, including in China.
There were also unsold cargoes from the influx three million tonnes of arbitrage cargoes from the West, with about seven sellers still seeking buyers.
Traders said this, as well as the return of refineries from maintenance shutdowns, have forced up Singapore middle-distillate stocks to at least a three-year record of 10.35 million barrels.
Traders also did not expect India's July diesel purchases to resuscitate the weak market, despite the relatively higher volumes expected for July.
They expected India to buy about 360,000 tonnes of 1.0-percent sulphur gas oil, and 180,000 tonnes each of the 0.5 and 0.25 percent sulphur grades in its tender closing May 27.
India had bought only 270,000 tonnes of 1.0-percent sulphur gas oil and 45,000 tonnes of the 0.25-percent sulphur grade for June.
Traders said jet fuel market was similarly well supplied as seen in the more than 15 offers made into Taiwan's tender to buy 32,000 tonnes of jet fuel last week.
The award at around $201 per tonne for July delivery, c-and-f basis, was lower than the last cargoes CPC bought for May delivery at $204 per tonne.
Weak demand seen for naphtha has extended its contango all the way until August, making it difficult for traders to reconcile the Saudi one-year term prices concluded last week, traders said.
Most buyers have agreed to pay a record premium of $17.00 per tonne over Saudi Aramco's formula for A-180 and $15 for low-paraffinic full-range material, they said.

Although higher gasoline domestic demand in China and South Korea during the summer months will dry up exports and provide support in the mid-term, current fundamentals were still bearish, as illustrated by Taiwan's low 95-octane unleaded reformate tender awards.
Traders had expected the latest awards at $24.92-$25.20 per barrel to be higher than CPC's last award at $25.30 because of rising crude values.
High sulphur 180-cst fuel oil has been capped at $103.50 per tonne, with a buyer who has bought at least five cargoes in the past two weeks, unwilling to bid up prices.
"The price is now at the high end," said one trader. "Demand is not significant except from the local buyer."
Firmer direction would emerge from Taiwan's fuel oil export tender for 30,000-tonnes of 3.0-percent sulphur fuel oil in June which closes on Monday, traders said.

LSWR prices are expected to firm with Indonesia's June allocation of 3.1 million barrels, lower than the 3.85 made in May, while summer demand from Japan, the main LSWR importer, to emerge in late May or early June.
